analysis.one_liner: Strengthens worker pensions and wages when their employer goes bankrupt and curbs executive payouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced by Senator Manchin in November 2022 with no cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change bankruptcy law so that when a company files for bankruptcy, it must keep funding its pension plan, and workers' unpaid wages and pension contributions would rank higher in line for payment, with the per-worker wage cap doubled from $10,000 to $20,000 and the 180-day time limit removed. It would stop courts from quickly approving sales of the whole company in the first 60 days unless the court finds value will collapse, and would require judges to consider whether a buyer keeps jobs and honors pension and retiree health obligations. It would also tighten limits on executive retention bonuses and insider payouts, and extend the window for clawing back fraudulent transfers from two years to six years.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees at companies that file for bankruptcy. Their back pay would be recouped up to twice the current amount and without the current 180-day cutoff, pension funds would get first-in-line repayment of missed contributions, and courts would have to weigh job and benefit preservation when selling the company. Retirees also gain from tighter limits on executive bonuses in bankrupt companies and a longer window for clawing back money siphoned out before a filing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority wage cap from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and removes the 180-day limit, so workers recoup more of their back pay when an employer goes bankrupt.
Requires companies to keep making minimum pension contributions and withdrawal-liability payments during bankruptcy, rather than pausing them while the case proceeds.

Bars bankruptcy courts from approving sales of substantially all company assets in the first 60 days unless the court finds value is likely to collapse, and requires courts to weigh whether a bidder will keep jobs and honor pension and retiree health obligations.
Extends the window for clawing back fraudulent transfers from two years to six years, reaching transfers made further in advance of the filing.

Tightens limits on executive retention bonuses and insider payouts, requiring clear and convincing evidence that the payments are essential and reasonable, and that they are not disproportionate to the concessions taken from the nonmanagement workforce.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate lenders and investors in distressed companies, who would recover less when a bankrupt employer owes pension contributions and withdrawal liability, and companies that would have to keep funding pensions and pay withdrawal liability during bankruptcy. Executives of bankrupt firms would face harder limits on retention bonuses and incentive pay.

drawbacks.text: Requiring companies to keep funding pensions and pay withdrawal liability during bankruptcy could push some distressed employers toward immediate liquidation rather than reorganization, potentially costing jobs.

Tightening sale-of-asset rules and extending the fraudulent-transfer look-back to six years could make it harder and more expensive to rescue failing companies, which critics would say can hurt the workers the bill aims to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers and retirees whose pensions now stand behind loans and executive pay in bankruptcies would have been real and significant; the main cost falls on lenders and private equity buyers, who would pay more for distressed companies and price that into lending. Some good-faith observers argue the restrictions on asset sales could make rescues of dying companies harder, hurting the very workers the bill protects, but the bill's core priority changes are targeted at well-documented abuses.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, it was never taken up and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Manchin introduced the SLAP Act on November 15, 2022, during the final weeks of the 117th Congress.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders, private equity buyers, and companies that might have faced higher pension obligations in bankruptcy are better off; workers and pension funds gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral, so it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No other senator signed on and no vote was ever taken, so no pattern of support or opposition emerged; the bill died in committee with zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and distressed-asset investors
industries.note: The bill raises the bar for buying companies out of bankruptcy and extends the window for clawing back pre-bankruptcy cash transfers, targeting practices that strip assets before a filing.
Some fee-generating strategies around quick asset sales and insider compensation would be curtailed, while the litigation over new standards could generate other work.

industries.industry: Bank lenders and other secured creditors
industries.note: Senior status for pension contributions and withdrawal liability pushes them further back in line in bankruptcies where pensions are underfunded.
Employers in these plans could no longer shed pension funding and withdrawal liability through bankruptcy, shifting costs back onto employers and away from the pension insurance system and retirees.
